hints: Look at the diagram: the marked $70.0^{\circ}$ is between the two first order beams, not between one beam and the central incident direction.
Recall the grating equation $d\sin\theta = n\lambda$ uses $\theta$ measured from the straight-through zero order to the $n$th order maximum.
For $n=1$, first halve $70.0^{\circ}$ to get $\theta$, then calculate $\lambda = d\sin\theta$ with $d = 1.00 \times 10^{-6} \text{ m}$.
walkthrough: The grating equation needs the angle of one diffracted order from the central axis. The diagram shows $70.0^{\circ}$ between the upper and lower first order maxima.
By symmetry the central axis bisects that angle, so $\theta = 70.0^{\circ}/2 = 35.0^{\circ}$ for $n=1$.
With $\sin35.0^{\circ} \approx 0.574$, $\lambda \approx 5.74 \times 10^{-7} \text{ m} = 574 \text{ nm}$, which checks as visible light. This is option C.

options.A: This is half the correct value, obtained if $d\sin\theta$ for $n=1$ is then divided by 2 again.
options.B: This does not follow from $d\sin35.0^{\circ}$ with $d = 1.00 \times 10^{-6} \text{ m}$ and $n=1$.
options.C: With $\theta = 35.0^{\circ}$ and $n=1$, $\lambda = d\sin\theta$ gives about $5.74 \times 10^{-7} \text{ m} = 574 \text{ nm}$.
options.D: This uses the full $70.0^{\circ}$ in $d\sin\theta$, giving $1.00 \times 10^{-6}\sin70.0^{\circ} \approx 940 \text{ nm}$.
